title: The happy life
hookLine: On the Happy Life: happiness is living in agreement with nature (On the Happy Life 3)
last: VIRTUS — WHAT DOES THIS ASK OF ME.

lines: FEW CAN SAY WHAT IT IS.
cards: Ask people what they want from life and the word happy keeps turning up. Ask what happiness actually is, and the answers scatter, along with a lot of shrugging.
Seneca wrote a whole book on this for his brother Gallio, and it opens right there. Everyone wants to live happily, he says, but when it comes to seeing what makes a life happy, they're in the dark.
So they follow the crowd, like sheep following the flock, going not where they should go but where everyone goes.

teach.b: First, don't follow the crowd. The most crowded, well-worn path, Seneca says, is the one most likely to mislead. Nothing gets us into more trouble than taking our lead from the rumor of what everyone else thinks.
Ask what is best, not what is usual. Second, the definition. In chapter three he gives the Stoic answer, the one he says all Stoics share.
I follow nature. Not to wander from it, and to shape yourself by its law and example: that is wisdom. A happy life is one in agreement with its own nature.
Third, what nature means here. Not the woods, exactly.

teach.h: A SOUND MIND, BRAVE AND PATIENT.
teach.b: Seneca fills it in at once: first, a sound mind that stays sound; then a brave and energetic one, patient, ready for whatever the times bring; careful of the body without fretting over it; using what fortune gives without becoming its slave.
Fourth, what it leaves out: wealth, fame, pleasure, luck. Seneca doesn't call them evil. He says they're not what happiness is made of.
A person can have them and be miserable, or lack them and be content.
The happy life is lived from the inside, in agreement with what you are, not handed to you by the crowd.

how: Some Stoic readers use 'living in agreement with nature' as a check on their choices, asking what a sound, steady mind would do rather than what everyone else does.

o: a quiet life lived far from the city
a life full of wealth, pleasure and luck
a life in agreement with its own nature

games.q: the happy life — tap the pairs.
p: a life in agreement with nature
the first mark of the happy life

s: Seneca says the well-worn path is the safest
he says the most crowded road is the one most likely to mislead.
Seneca says the definition of the happy life is shared by all Stoics
he says: I follow nature, as all Stoics agree.
Seneca says wealth and pleasure are evil
he says they're not what happiness is made of.

games.q: you want to be happy, and everyone around you is heading the same way. what's Seneca's first advice?
o: follow them; crowds are usually right.
ask what is best, not what is usual.
go the opposite way on principle.
games.why: he warns that the most traveled road misleads most, and that following the flock is how we get lost.

practice: Ask yourself, gently, what agreement with your nature would look like in the next hour: water because you're thirsty, a step outside after a day indoors, one clear thought instead of twenty scrolls.
Let one simple, natural thing come to mind, and picture doing it, unhurried. Notice how little it costs.

wordCard.voice: Beata vita. Latin for the happy life: not what the crowd chases, but a life in agreement with its own nature, sound of mind and brave. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, 'the happy life': the title of Seneca's book to his brother Gallio.

carryVoice: Your line: in agreement. Best and usual aren't always the same road. See you tomorrow.
